# How early can a ground team trust a landing time? A pilot study at Frankfurt

> **Pilot study.** One evening of live OpenSky data, 2026-10-18 17:45:52 CEST to 2026-10-19 03:37:12 CEST (9.9 hours). 120 arrivals kept, 24 in the held-out test set. The collector keeps running, so later runs will cover more days.

*Generated by `run.py` from `results/results.json`. Research demo. Not for operational use.*

## Abstract

Ground teams at an A-CDM airport plan stands and handling around the estimated landing time. They need to know from when that estimate can be trusted, not only how accurate it is on average. We study this for arrivals at Frankfurt (EDDF) with open OpenSky ADS-B data. A LightGBM quantile model predicts time to touchdown, and conformalized quantile regression calibrates the interval per distance band to 80 percent target coverage. For each flight we define the trust point as the earliest prediction from which every later interval is no wider than a window W and contains the true touchdown. In this pilot of 9.9 hours of live data, 24 held-out test flights had a median trust lead of 7.2 minutes at W = 5 minutes, against 0.0 minutes for an empirical baseline. The median paired difference was 7.2 minutes (95% interval 4.8 to 7.8). The study is small and grows as the collector keeps running.

## 1. Introduction

In Airport Collaborative Decision Making (A-CDM), the estimated landing time (ELDT) feeds the estimated in-block time, stand and gate planning, and the target off-block time of the next departure. The EUROCONTROL A-CDM manual names both the accuracy and the timeliness of ELDT as performance indicators. A ground team needs both at once: an estimate that is accurate on average but still moves in the last minutes forces late decisions.

We ask how early a ground team at Frankfurt can trust a landing time. We answer with a prediction interval and a per-flight trust point. Earlier work predicts landing time well (for example DFS AMAN, FlightAware Foresight, and research models at Dallas/Fort Worth and Incheon) and some work gives intervals (Glina et al. 2012, Kim, Yoon and Lee 2025). We did not find a study that measures when the interval for one flight becomes both narrow and correct. The full review is in `docs/related_work.md`.

## 2. Data

We polled the OpenSky Network REST API for state vectors around Frankfurt from 2026-10-18 17:45:52 CEST to 2026-10-19 03:37:12 CEST. This gave 431659 state vectors from 1944 aircraft. We split tracks into 2852 flights and kept 120 arrivals.

Drop reasons: not_arrival_no_touchdown 2408, gap_over_120s_inside_20nm 64, too_few_points 241, not_arrival_never_airborne_beyond_30nm 19. Label methods: ground_extrapolated 76, ground_midpoint 33, fallback_extrapolated 11. Landing directions: 07 102, unk 16, 25 2.

Fewer than 3 local days had 150 or more arrivals, so flights were sorted by touchdown time and split into blocks: first 60.0 percent train, next 20.0 percent calibration, the rest test. Train: 72 flights, 2026-10-18 16:03:55 UTC to 2026-10-18 18:29:21 UTC; Calibration: 24 flights, 2026-10-18 18:32:20 UTC to 2026-10-18 19:42:05 UTC; Test: 24 flights, 2026-10-18 19:42:55 UTC to 2026-10-18 21:56:04 UTC.

## 3. Method

1. Collect OpenSky state vectors around Frankfurt with `collect_live.py`.
2. Split tracks into flights after gaps over 15 minutes. Keep arrivals seen beyond 30 nm that touch down within 5 nm of the airport.
3. Label touchdown from the first ground report, or extrapolate from the last airborne point when the gap is long or there is no ground report.
4. Build features from data at or before each prediction time: position, speed, altitude changes, turning, recent landing direction and traffic.
5. Train LightGBM quantile models (0.1, 0.5, 0.9) on the train flights.
6. Calibrate with conformalized quantile regression on the calibration flights, per distance band, to 80 percent target coverage.
7. On the test flights, find the trust point for W = 2, 5, 10 minutes and compare with baseline B (quantiles of time to touchdown by 5 nm distance bin and landing direction).

**Baselines.** Baseline A divides distance by ground speed. Baseline B takes empirical quantiles of time to touchdown in training, by distance bin and recent landing direction, and gets the same conformal correction as the model.

**Further statistics.** The interval score and the pinball loss are proper scores [gneiting2007strictly], so they reward intervals that are both narrow and correct. We also report paired point error per flight, quantile reliability and coverage per split.

**Statistics.** All intervals come from 10000 bootstrap resamples of whole test flights, because rows inside a flight are not independent. The paired comparison uses a Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

**Hypotheses.**

* H1 not supported. Calibrated coverage (%) by band: 0 to 20 nm 74.9, 20 to 50 nm 66.9, 50 to 100 nm 70.2, over 100 nm 71.7. Uncalibrated: 0 to 20 nm 55.2, 20 to 50 nm 28.4, 50 to 100 nm 25.1, over 100 nm 39.1. Target 80 ± 5 points, bands with at least 50 test rows.
* H2 supported. Median paired difference in trust lead at W = 5 min, model minus baseline B: 7.2 min, 95% bootstrap interval 4.8 to 7.8 min, 24 flights, Wilcoxon p = 1.19e-07.
* H3 not supported. Median trust lead 5.2 min in the quietest traffic tercile (8 flights) and 6.9 min in the busiest (8 flights). Difference quiet minus busy -1.7 min, 95% interval -14.8 to 2.6.
* H4 unclear. 1 test flight with holding, 23 without (minimum for a test: 5).

### 4.1 Further statistics

These are exploratory. They explain the hypothesis results and do not change any verdict.

**Who wins per flight.** At W = 5 minutes the model gave a longer trust lead than baseline B on 100.0 percent of test flights, a tie on 0.0 percent and a shorter lead on 0.0 percent. The mean gain was 7.9 (6.0 to 10.3) minutes.

**Interval score.** The interval score adds the width of the interval and a penalty for each miss, so lower is better and a narrow interval cannot win by missing. Over all test rows the model scored 6.8 minutes against 10.5 for baseline B, a difference of -3.7 (-6.2 to -0.6) minutes.

**Calibration drift.** The conformal step reached 80.2 percent coverage on the calibration flights, as it should by design, but 71.1 percent (95% CI 60.1 to 81.4) on the test flights, which landed later in the evening. On the train flights coverage was 99.7 percent: the quantile model fits its own training flights much more tightly than new flights. Both facts point the same way. The gap between calibration and test is the main reason H1 fails, and more days of data, split by day, is the fix.

## 5. Discussion

At W = 5 minutes the model gave a longer trust lead than baseline B, and the bootstrap interval of the paired difference lies above zero.

0.0 percent of test flights were never trusted by the calibrated model at W = 5 minutes, against 100.0 percent for baseline B. The trust point is strict: one late miss resets it, and an interval built to miss a share of rows will often miss close to touchdown.

H1 is not supported. Calibration on one block of the evening does not guarantee coverage on the next block when traffic changes.

H3 and H4 depend on small groups in a pilot of one evening. Their verdicts (not supported and unclear) should be read as a first look.

## 6. Limitations

* One evening of data. The test set is small and covers one part of one day.
* The split is a time block inside the same evening, not separate days.
* OpenSky relies on volunteer receivers, so coverage near the ground has gaps.
* Touchdown is inferred from ADS-B, not taken from an official landing time, so labels carry noise.
* Inbound status of other aircraft is taken as known, like a flight plan, for the traffic features.
* Conformal coverage is marginal: it holds on average over rows, not for each flight.

## 7. Future work

* Run the collector over many days and split by day, as the pipeline already does once enough days exist.
* Use the OpenSky Trino history to train and test over months.
* Add weather, for example METAR wind, which drives runway choice and approach speed.
* Regularise the quantile model more strongly. Train coverage near one hundred percent shows it fits its own flights too tightly. Any such change must be chosen on train and calibration flights only, never on test.
* Recalibrate on a rolling window of recent flights to follow drift through the evening.
* Repeat the study at more airports.
